items.title: The weak and soft overcome the hard and strong.
items.rule: Reversal is how the Way moves; weakness is how the Way is used. The hard and strong go with death and the soft and weak with life. Nothing is softer than water, yet nothing does better at attacking the hard: everyone knows the weak beats the strong, and no one can practise it.
items.words: 反者道之動，弱者道之用。 — "Reversal is the movement of the Way; weakness is the use of the Way." (ch. 40) · 故堅強者死之徒，柔弱者生之徒。是以兵強則不勝… 強大處下，柔弱處上。 — "So the hard and strong are companions of death, the soft and weak companions of life. So when an army is strong it does not win… The strong and great sit below; the soft and weak sit above." (ch. 76) · 天下莫柔弱於水，而攻堅強者，莫之能勝，其無以易之。弱之勝強，柔之勝剛，天下莫不知莫能行。是以聖人云：「受國之垢，是謂社稷主；受國不祥，是為天下王。」正言若反。 — "Nothing in the world is softer and weaker than water, yet for attacking the hard and strong nothing surpasses it; nothing can take its place. That the weak beats the strong and the soft beats the hard, everyone in the world knows and no one can practise. So the sage says: 'One who takes on the state's filth is called lord of its altars; one who takes on the state's misfortune is king of the world.' Straight words seem reversed." (ch. 78) Guodian 甲: 返也者，道○（动）也。溺（弱）也者，道之○（用）也。 (ch. 40)
items.source: 道德經 chs. 40, 76, 78 (王弼本); 郭店 甲 37 (ch. 40 only; chs. 76 and 78 are not in Guodian). Silk ch. 4 (`silk.txt:54`), ch. 41 (`:435`), and ch. 43 (`:455–457`: 水之勝剛 弱之勝強 天下莫弗知 而莫能行也).
items.label: `quoted`

items.title: What is to be shrunk must first be stretched.
items.rule: What is to be shrunk must first be stretched; what is to be weakened must first be strengthened. What is to be discarded must first be raised (WB 廢/興; silk 去/與, "given to"), and what is to be taken must first be given. This is called subtle clarity (微明). The words do not say who does the stretching or what follows.
items.words: 將欲歙之，必固張之；將欲弱之，必固強之；將欲廢之，必固興之；將欲奪之，必固與之。是謂微明。柔弱勝剛強。魚不可脫於淵，國之利器不可以示人。 — "About to shrink it, one must first stretch it; about to weaken it, one must first strengthen it; about to abolish it, one must first raise it; about to seize it, one must first give to it. This is called subtle clarity. The soft and weak beat the hard and strong. Fish must not leave the deep; the state's sharp instruments must not be shown to people." Silk A: 將欲拾之，必古張之；將欲弱之，□□強之；將欲去之，必古與之；將欲奪之，必古予之。是胃微明。柔弱勝強。魚不脫於瀟，邦利器不可以視人。
items.source: 道德經 ch. 36 (王弼本); silk ch. 80 (`silk.txt:882–886`; A as quoted, from the 帛書本 page). Not in Guodian. 韓非子·喻老 reads it as strategy: 越王入宦於吳…故曰：「將欲翕之，必固張之」 and 晉獻公將欲襲虞，遺之以璧馬…故曰：「將欲取之，必固與之。」 That is Han Fei's application, not the text's words.
items.label: `quoted`

items.title: Achieve the result and stop; use weapons when it cannot be avoided; mourn the victory.
items.rule: One who helps a ruler by the Way does not use troops to force the world. The good one achieves the result and stops, and does not use it to take strength. He achieves it without vaunting, boasting or arrogance, and as something he could not avoid. Weapons are instruments of ill omen, used when there is no alternative; calm indifference is best, victory is not made beautiful, and a victory is treated with the rites of mourning.
items.words: 以道佐人主者，不以兵強天下。其事好還。…善有果而已，不敢以取強。果而勿矜，果而勿伐，果而勿驕。果而不得已，果而勿強。 — "One who assists a ruler with the Way does not force the world with troops; such affairs tend to come back. … The good one has a result and that is all; he does not dare use it to take strength. Result, and no vaunting; result, and no boasting; result, and no arrogance; result, as something unavoidable; result, and no forcing." (ch. 30) · 兵者不祥之器，非君子之器，不得已而用之，恬淡為上。勝而不美，而美之者，是樂殺人。…戰勝，以喪禮處之。 — "Weapons are instruments of ill omen, not the gentleman's instruments; when it cannot be avoided he uses them, and calm indifference is best. He wins and does not find it beautiful; one who finds it beautiful delights in killing people. … A victory in war is handled with the rites of mourning." (ch. 31) Guodian 甲: 以○（道）差（佐）人○（主）者，不谷（欲）以兵强于天下。善者果而已，不以取强。果而弗发（伐），果而弗乔（骄），果而弗○（矜），是胃（谓）果而不强。 (ch. 30) · Guodian 丙: …得已而甬（用）之。○○为上，弗○（美）也。○〈美〉之，是乐杀人。…战○（胜）则以丧豊（礼）居之。 (ch. 31)
items.source: 道德經 chs. 30, 31 (王弼本); 郭店 甲 6–8 (ch. 30), 丙 6–10 (ch. 31); silk chs. 74, 75 (`silk.txt:806–833`). WB has no commentary on ch. 31. 晁說之's postface in the sources file reports that Wang Bi took 佳兵者不祥之器…以喪禮處之 as 非老子之言, yet Guodian 丙 and both silk copies carry it.
items.label: `quoted`

items.title: Do not display yourself; do not contend.
items.kind: decision rule (four parallel restraints, no order)
items.rule: Bent, then whole; crooked, then straight; hollow, then full; worn, then new; little, then gaining; much, then confused. The sage does not display himself and so is clear, does not affirm himself and so stands out, does not boast and so has merit, and does not vaunt himself and so lasts; because he does not contend, no one in the world can contend with him.
items.words: 曲則全，枉則直，窪則盈，敝則新，少則得，多則惑。是以聖人抱一為天下式。不自見故明，不自是故彰，不自伐故有功，不自矜故長。夫唯不爭，故天下莫能與之爭。 — "Bent, then whole; crooked, then straight; hollow, then full; worn, then new; little, then gained; much, then confused. So the sage embraces the one and is the world's model. Not displaying himself, he is clear; not affirming himself, he is distinguished; not boasting, he has merit; not vaunting, he lasts. Just because he does not contend, no one in the world can contend with him." (ch. 22) · 企者不立，跨者不行，自見者不明，自是者不彰，自伐者無功，自矜者不長。其在道也，曰餘食贅行。物或惡之，故有道者不處。 — "On tiptoe one does not stand; striding, one does not walk. Who displays himself is not clear; who affirms himself is not distinguished; who boasts has no merit; who vaunts does not last. In the Way these are called leftover food and superfluous action. Things may loathe them, so one who has the Way does not dwell in them." (ch. 24)
items.source: 道德經 chs. 22, 24 (王弼本). Silk ch. 67 = received 22 (`silk.txt:715–721`, 執一以為天下牧) and silk ch. 66 = received 24 (`:708–710`, 炊者不立). The 明/彰 pairing swaps between silk A (不□視故明，不自見故章, one graph lost) and silk B (不自視故章，不自見也故明). Neither chapter is in Guodian.
items.label: `quoted`

items.title: The highest good is like water.
items.rule: The highest good is like water: water benefits all things and does not contend (WB), and it settles where people dislike to be, so it is near the Way. Good in dwelling is the ground, in the heart depth, in giving benevolence (silk B: heaven), in speech trust, in governing order, in affairs ability, and in moving timing; because it does not contend, there is no blame.
items.words: 上善若水。水善利萬物而不爭，處眾人之所惡，故幾於道。居善地，心善淵，與善仁，言善信，正善治，事善能，動善時。夫唯不爭，故無尤。 — "The highest good is like water. Water is good at benefiting the ten thousand things and does not contend; it settles where the crowd dislikes, and so it is near the Way. Dwelling: good is the ground. Heart: good is depth. Giving: good is benevolence. Speech: good is trust. Governing: good is order. Affairs: good is ability. Moving: good is timing. Just because it does not contend, there is no blame." Silk A: 上善治水﹦善利萬物而有靜…夫唯不靜，故無尤. Silk B: 上善如水﹦善利萬物而有爭…予善天，言善信…夫唯不爭，故無尤.
items.source: 道德經 ch. 8 (王弼本); silk ch. 52 (`silk.txt:550–554`, a composite of A and B); 帛書本 page for A and B. Not in Guodian. Where WB has 而不爭, both silk copies have 而有—. A uses 靜 also for the closing 不爭, so the silk's sense at this point is unresolved (my reading).
items.label: `quoted`

items.title: Knowing yourself is clarity; overcoming yourself is strength.
items.kind: mindset (eight parallel statements, not a ladder)
items.rule: Knowing others is cleverness; knowing yourself is clarity. Overcoming others takes force and overcoming yourself is strength; knowing what is enough is wealth, pressing on is will, not losing your place is lasting, and dying without perishing is long life.
items.words: 知人者智，自知者明。勝人者有力，自勝者強。知足者富。強行者有志。不失其所者久。死而不亡者壽。 — "One who knows others is clever; one who knows himself is clear. One who overcomes others has force; one who overcomes himself is strong. One who knows what is enough is rich. One who presses on has will. One who does not lose his place lasts. One who dies and does not perish is long-lived."
items.source: 道德經 ch. 33 (王弼本); silk ch. 77 (`silk.txt:851–857`: 知人者 知也 … 死不忘者 壽也; silk B 死而不忘者壽也, "dies and is not forgotten"). Not in Guodian.
items.label: `quoted`

items.title: The use is in what is not there.
items.rule: The cart's use is in the empty space at the hub, the vessel's use in its hollow, and the room's use in the openings. So what is there gives benefit, and what is not there gives use. The words do not say to remove anything; that would be an application.
items.words: 三十輻共一轂，當其無，有車之用。埏埴以為器，當其無，有器之用。鑿戶牖以為室，當其無，有室之用。故有之以為利，無之以為用。 — "Thirty spokes share one hub; in its nothing lies the cart's use. Clay is moulded into a vessel; in its nothing lies the vessel's use. Doors and windows are cut to make a room; in its nothing lies the room's use. So what is there makes for benefit; what is not there makes for use."
items.source: 道德經 ch. 11 (王弼本); silk ch. 55 (`silk.txt:583–589`). Not in Guodian.
items.label: `quoted`

items.title: When your time comes, ride out; when it does not, drift away.
items.rule: A gentleman who gets his time rides out, and one who does not drifts away. The good merchant hides his goods deep as if he had none, and the gentleman of full virtue looks like a fool. Confucius is told to put away his arrogance and many desires, his airs and excessive aims, which do his person no good. Separately, as narrator, Sima Qian writes that Laozi's learning made hiding himself and namelessness its task, and that, seeing Zhou decline, he left.
items.words: 老子曰：「子所言者，其人與骨皆已朽矣，獨其言在耳。且君子得其時則駕，不得其時則蓬累而行。吾聞之，良賈深藏若虛，君子盛德容貌若愚。去子之驕氣與多欲，態色與淫志，是皆無益於子之身。吾所以告子，若是而已。」 — "Laozi said: 'The men you speak of have rotted, they and their bones; only their words remain. And a gentleman, when he gets his time, rides out; when he does not get his time, he goes off like drifting tumbleweed. I have heard that a good merchant stores deep as if empty, and a gentleman of abundant virtue looks like a fool. Get rid of your arrogance and many desires, your airs and wanton ambition; none of these benefits your person. What I have to tell you is this, and only this.'" · Narrator: 老子修道德，其學以自隱無名為務。居周久之，見周之衰，乃遂去。 — "Laozi cultivated the Way and virtue; his learning made hiding himself and having no name its task. He lived long in Zhou; seeing Zhou's decline, he then left."
items.source: 史記 卷63 老子韓非列傳 (`sources/lao-tzu/史記_卷063.txt` lines 13, 15). Line 21 is Sima Qian on the identification: 世莫知其然否.
items.label: `attributed`. The speech is Sima Qian's report of Laozi speaking to Confucius; the second part is the narrator's voice.

items.title: Where others take the front, take the rear; restraint as the rule.
items.rule: Where everyone takes the front, he alone takes the rear, saying he takes on the world's reproach (variant: filth). Where everyone takes the solid, he alone takes the empty, and where everyone seeks good fortune, he alone stays bent and whole, saying "just escape blame". He takes depth as the root and restraint (約) as the rule, saying "the hard is broken, the sharp is blunted".
items.words: 老耼曰：「知其雄，守其雌，爲天下谿。知其白，守其辱，爲天下谷。」人皆取先，己獨取後，曰：「受天下之詬（一作垢）。」人皆取實，己獨取虛。无藏也，故有餘，巋然而有餘。其行身也，徐而不費，无爲也而笑巧。人皆求福，己獨曲全，曰：「苟免於咎。」以深爲根，以約爲紀，曰：「堅則毀矣，銳則挫矣。」常寬容於物，不削於人。 — "Lao Dan said: 'Know the male, keep to the female, and be the world's ravine; know the white, keep to the disgraced, and be the world's valley.' Everyone takes the front; he alone takes the rear, saying: 'Take on the world's reproach' (variant: filth). Everyone takes the solid; he alone takes the empty. Hoarding nothing, he has more than enough, abundantly. In conducting himself he is slow and not wasteful; he does nothing and laughs at cleverness. Everyone seeks good fortune; he alone keeps bent and whole, saying: 'Just escape blame.' He takes depth as the root and restraint as the rule, saying: 'The hard is broken; the sharp is blunted.' He is always tolerant of things and does not pare away at people."
items.source: 莊子·天下, the paragraph on 關尹 and 老耼 ([zh.wikisource 莊子/天下](https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/莊子/天下)).
items.label: `attributed`. This is the 天下 author's description, with sayings he attributes to Lao Dan. The paragraph opens with 關尹 and 老耼 together; the lines after 老耼曰 are read as about Lao Dan (my reading of the paragraph's order). 知其雄…為天下谷 matches 道德經 ch. 28; 受…詬/垢 echoes ch. 78's 受國之垢; 曲全 echoes ch. 22.

who.markdown: Linus Benedict Torvalds (born 28 December 1969 in Helsinki, Finland; Swedish-speaking Finn, naturalised US citizen 2010) has been the creator and lead developer of the Linux kernel since 1991. He announced his "free operating system … just a hobby" for 386/486 AT clones on comp.os.minix on 25 August 1991 (Message-ID `1991Aug25.205708.9541@klaava.Helsinki.FI`), released 1.0 on 14 March 1994, and relicensed the kernel under the GPLv2 after hearing Richard Stallman speak in the autumn of 1991 (Wikipedia, *Linus Torvalds*, citing *Torvalds & Diamond, Just for Fun*, and comp.os.minix; *The early days of Linux*, Lars Wirzenius, LWN). He worked at Transmeta from February 1997 to June 2003, then at OSDL and the Linux Foundation, and moved to Oregon in 2004. In 2005, after the BitKeeper dispute, he wrote Git starting 3 April 2005 and handed it to Junio Hamano by mid-2005; Git exists because "the Linux kernel developers needed a tool they could use to version the kernel". He wrote very little of the kernel himself — about 2% as of 2006 — and said in 2012 that his own contribution is now "mostly merging code written by others". What he kept was the last word: `Documentation/process/submitting-patches.rst` states, in the present tense, "Linus Torvalds is the final arbiter of all changes accepted into the Linux kernel", while noting that "very few patches go through Linus directly". He codified how he would exercise that power in prose rather than edicts — `Documentation/process/management-style.rst` ("This is a short document describing the preferred (or made up, depending on who you ask) management style for the linux kernel") and the much older `coding-style.rst` ("this is what goes for anything that I have to be able to maintain"). In September 2018, after The New Yorker reported on his years of abusive mailing-list mail, he replaced the kernel's Code of Conflict with a Code of Conduct, called his past attacks "unprofessional and uncalled for", took time off to work on how he responds to people, and returned to maintaining 4.19 in October 2018. Awards: 2012 Millennium Technology Prize, 2014 IEEE Computer Pioneer Award, 2018 IEEE Masaru Ibuka Consumer Electronics Award.

items.title: A change that breaks what used to work for users is a kernel bug: fix it or revert it, in the kernel, and admit it.
items.rule:
If a change makes user programs break, the bug is in the kernel, not in the user program. The change
must be fixed or reverted, and fixed in the kernel. When a regression happens, it is admitted and fixed instead of
blamed on user space. If the kernel used to work for you, it continues to work for you. He says there have been
exceptions, but "few and far between". For API breakage inside the kernel: whoever broke something fixes it too.
items.words:
(English original)
- "If a change results in user programs breaking, it's a bug in the kernel. We never EVER blame the user programs." … "WE DO NOT BREAK USERSPACE!"
- "The first rule is: - we don't cause regressions and the corollary is that when regressions *do* occur, we admit to them and fix them, instead of blaming user space."
- "If the kernel used to work for you, the rule is that it continues to work for you. There have been exceptions, but they are few and far between, and they generally have some major and fundamental reasons for having happened, that were basically entirely unavoidable, and people _tried_hard_ to avoid them."
- "But if something actually breaks, then the change must get fixed or reverted. And it gets fixed in the *kernel*."
- "Nobody can say "I now broke the API you used, and now _you_ need to fix it up". Whoever broke something gets to fix it too."
items.source:
LKML, 23 Dec 2012, "Re: [Regression w/ patch] Media commit causes user space to misbahave (was: Re:
Linux 3.8-rc1)", https://lkml.org/lkml/2012/12/23/75 · LKML, 26 Oct 2017, "Re: regression in 4.14-rc2 caused
by apparmor: add base infastructure for socket mediation",
https://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/1710.3/02474.html and …/1710.3/02487.html
items.label: `quoted`

items.title: Talk is cheap; show the code.
items.rule:
A claim that something can be built costs nothing to make; what he asks for is the code. In 2017 he
did not accept a main pull request because its untested code "clearly didn't do what it claimed it did".
items.words:
(English original)
- "Talk is cheap. Show me the code." (his whole reply to Jamie Lokier's claim that the best of user-space and
  kernel threads could be combined "in less than 8kB per thread")
- "untested code that clearly didn't do what it claimed it did, and which caused me to not even accept the main pull request"
items.source:
LKML, 25 Aug 2000, "Re: SCO: "thread creation is about a thousand times faster than on native
Linux"", https://lkml.org/lkml/2000/8/25/132 · LKML, 26 Oct 2017, same apparmor thread,
https://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/1710.3/02507.html
items.label: `quoted`
items.from: new (my research). This is the line `design.md` builds the Linus seat on; this is its primary source.

items.title: What counts as a regression is a user's breakage, not an ABI, a document or a test.
items.rule:
A regression is the kernel not giving the same end result with the same user space. The rule is about
breaking a user's workflow. It is not about documented behaviour, about where the code lives, or about behaviour
never changing. A test that now behaves differently is a warning sign, not by itself a regression. Changing an
API is fine as long as nobody notices.
items.words:
(English original)
- "As far as the kernel is concerned, a regressions is THE KERNEL NOT GIVING THE SAME END RESULT WITH THE SAME USER SPACE." (2017)
- "The rules about regressions have never been about any kind of documented behavior, or where the code lives. The rules about regressions are always about "breaks user workflow". Users are literally the _only_ thing that matters." (2020)
- "And our regression rule has never been "behavior doesn't change". That would mean that we could never make any changes at all." (2017)
- "But if you have some random test that now behaves differently, it's not a regression. It's a *warning* sign, sure: tests are useful." (2024)
- "You can make any changes to an API you like - as long as nobody notices." (2020/2021, see Gaps)
items.source:
2017 line: LKML 26 Oct 2017, https://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/1710.3/02474.html (opened).
The others: his mails as reproduced in `Documentation/process/handling-regressions.rst`, "Quotes from Linus
about regression" (https://docs.kernel.org/process/handling-regressions.html), entries 2020-05-21, 2017-11-05,
"2024-29-01" and 2021-05-21, each with its lore.kernel.org link (originals not opened).
items.label: `quoted`

items.title: Avoid having to make the big decisions; the people who know the details should not need you to pick.
items.rule:
The aim is to avoid having to make decisions, at least the big and painful ones. If people you manage
ask you to choose (a) or (b) on a technical matter, you are in trouble: they should know the details better than
you, so you are not competent to decide it for them. If they don't know the details better than you, you are in
the wrong job. Small, non-consequential decisions are fine. The job is to turn the big and painful ones into small
things.
items.words:
(English original) "The name of the game is to avoid having to make a decision. In particular,
if somebody tells you "choose (a) or (b), we really need you to decide on this", you're in trouble as a manager.
The people you manage had better know the details better than you, so if they come to you for a technical
decision, you're screwed. You're clearly not competent to make that decision for them." … "So the name of the
game is to avoid decisions, at least the big and painful ones. Making small and non-consequential decisions is
fine, and makes you look like you know what you're doing, so what a kernel manager needs to do is to turn the big
and painful ones into small things where nobody really cares."
items.source:
`Documentation/process/management-style.rst` §1 "Decisions",
https://docs.kernel.org/process/management-style.html. The same text is in LWN, 6 Oct 2004, "Linus on kernel
management style", https://lwn.net/Articles/105375/
items.label: `quoted`. Authorship is by attribution only (see Gaps).

items.title: A decision is big only if it can't be undone; avoid doing things that can't be undone.
items.rule:
What separates a big decision from a small one is whether you can fix it afterwards. Any decision can be
made small by making sure that, if you were wrong (and you will be wrong), you can undo the damage by
backtracking. So avoid doing things that can't be undone. Deleting the work is easy, but you may have irrevocably
lost the trust of the engineer who did it, and then the decision was a big one after all.
items.words:
(English original) "It helps to realize that the key difference between a big decision and a
small one is whether you can fix your decision afterwards. Any decision can be made small by just always making
sure that if you were wrong (and you will be wrong), you can always undo the damage later by backtracking." …
"Thus the key to avoiding big decisions becomes to just avoiding to do things that can't be undone. Don't get
ushered into a corner from which you cannot escape." … "while the actual work was easy enough to undo by just
deleting it, you may have irrevocably lost the trust of that engineer. And remember: "irrevocable" was what we
tried to avoid in the first place, and your decision ended up being a big one after all."
items.source: `management-style.rst` §1 "Decisions"; LWN 2004 (as #4)
items.label: `quoted`. Authorship is by attribution only (see Gaps).

items.title: Let people smarter than you make the decisions; prod, don't push too hard.
items.rule:
Take advantage of smart people: they can make your decisions for you. When you find somebody smarter
than you, coast along, and your job becomes saying "Sounds like a good idea - go wild" or "That sounds good, but
what about xxx?". Greatness in one area does not necessarily carry over to others. You may prod people in a
direction, which is not irreversible because people drift back to what they are good at, but don't push too hard.
items.words:
(English original) "Some people react badly to smart people. Others take advantage of them.
Make sure that you, as a kernel maintainer, are in the second group. Suck up to them, because they are the people
who will make your job easier. In particular, they'll be able to make your decisions for you, which is what the
game is all about." … "So when you find somebody smarter than you are, just coast along. Your management
responsibilities largely become ones of saying "Sounds like a good idea - go wild", or "That sounds good, but what
about xxx?"." … "One thing to look out for is to realize that greatness in one area does not necessarily translate
to other areas. So you might prod people in specific directions, but let's face it, they might be good at what
they do, and suck at everything else. The good news is that people tend to naturally gravitate back to what they
are good at, so it's not like you are doing something irreversible when you do prod them in some direction, just
don't push too hard."
items.source: `management-style.rst` §3 "People II - the Good Kind"; LWN 2004
items.label: `quoted`. Authorship is by attribution only (see Gaps).

items.title: Say up front that you may be wrong; give people critical thinking, not confidence.
items.rule:
Admit up front that you don't know. Tell people ahead of time that your decision is preliminary and
might be wrong, keep the right to change your mind, and make sure they know it. If the people doing the work
aren't sure their work is a good idea, don't encourage them by promising it will be included; make them think
twice before a big endeavour. The best thing a manager can do is give them a healthy dose of critical thinking
about what they do, not confidence. And you are one of the idiots too.
items.words:
(English original, in source order) "Happily, both of these reasons can be mitigated
effectively by just admitting up-front that you don't have a friggin' clue, and telling people ahead of the fact
that your decision is purely preliminary, and might be the wrong thing. You should always reserve the right to
change your mind, and make people very aware of that." … "After all, if they aren't certain whether it's a good
idea, you sure as hell shouldn't encourage them by promising them that what they work on will be included. Make
them at least think twice before they embark on a big endeavor." … "The best thing you can do as a manager is not
to instill confidence, but rather a healthy dose of critical thinking on what they do." … (§3) "While it turns out
that most people are idiots, the corollary to that is sadly that you are one too"
items.source: `management-style.rst` §1 "Decisions", §3 "People II - the Good Kind"; LWN 2004
items.label: `quoted`. Authorship is by attribution only (see Gaps).

items.title: When it isn't clear which of two approaches is better, ask "can't we just do both?"
items.rule:
Another way to avoid a decision is to ask "can't we just do both?". If it is not clear which approach is
better, the people involved will eventually figure it out. Sometimes both teams give up. He reads that as usually
a sign that both projects had something wrong with them, and that they couldn't decide because both were wrong.
items.words:
(English original) "Btw, another way to avoid a decision is to plaintively just whine "can't we
just do both?" and look pitiful. Trust me, it works. If it's not clear which approach is better, they'll
eventually figure it out. The answer may end up being that both teams get so frustrated by the situation that they
just give up." … "That may sound like a failure, but it's usually a sign that there was something wrong with both
projects, and the reason the people involved couldn't decide was that they were both wrong."
items.source: `management-style.rst` §1 "Decisions"; LWN 2004
items.label: `quoted`. Authorship is by attribution only (see Gaps).

items.title: Design the code around the data, not the other way round.
items.rule:
He favours designing code around the data rather than the reverse, and gives it as one reason git
worked. He claims the difference between a bad programmer and a good one is whether they treat their code or
their data structures as more important.
items.words:
(English original) "In fact, I'm a huge proponent of designing your code around the data,
rather than the other way around, and I think it's one of the reasons git has been fairly successful (*)." …
"(*) I will, in fact, claim that the difference between a bad programmer and a good one is whether he considers
his code or his data structures more important. Bad programmers worry about the code. Good programmers worry
about data structures and their relationships."
items.source:
git mailing list, 27 Jul 2006, "Re: Licensing and the library version of git", Message-ID
`Pine.LNX.4.64.0607270936200.4168@g5.osdl.org`, https://marc.info/?l=git&m=115401850825206&w=2 (also LWN Quote
of the week, 29 Jul 2006, https://lwn.net/Articles/193244/)
items.label: `quoted`

items.title: Good code: see the problem differently so the special case becomes the normal case.
items.rule:
Sometimes you can see a problem in a different way and rewrite it so that a special case goes away and
becomes the normal case, and he calls that good code. The sign of people he wants to work with is good taste,
which is about seeing the big patterns and knowing by instinct the right way to do things.
items.words:
(English original, spoken; about two ways to remove an entry from a singly linked list) "I
want you to understand that sometimes you can see a problem in a different way and rewrite it so that a special
case goes away and becomes the normal case. And that's good code." … "To me, the sign of people I really want to
work with is that they have good taste" … "Good taste is about really seeing the big patterns and kind of
instinctively knowing what's the right way to do things."
items.source:
TED2016, "The mind behind Linux" (interview with Chris Anderson), transcript at
https://www.ted.com/talks/linus_torvalds_the_mind_behind_linux/transcript
items.label: `quoted` (spoken, as TED's transcript gives it)

items.title: A pull must tell him what he is pulling and why, as a record that will last; anything odd or late must be explained.
items.rule:
To him, the message is the important part. He wants to understand what he is pulling and why he should pull it. The
message becomes the merge message, so it must also make sense as a historical record. Anything odd belongs in the
explanation. If you touch files you don't maintain, explain why; he will see it in the diffstat anyway, and if it
isn't mentioned he gets extra suspicious. For anything sent after the merge window, or fixes that look scary,
explain what it does, why, and the timing.
items.words:
(English original) "Anyway, at least to me, the important part is the *message*. I want to
understand what I'm pulling, and why I should pull it. I also want to use that message as the message for the
merge, so it should not just make sense to me, but make sense as a historical record too. Note that if there is
something odd about the pull request, that should very much be in the explanation. If you're touching files that
you don't maintain, explain _why_. I will see it in the diffstat anyway, and if you didn't mention it, I'll just
be extra suspicious. And when you send me new stuff after the merge window (or even bug-fixes, but ones that look
scary), explain not just what they do and why they do it, but explain the _timing_. What happened that this
didn't go through the merge window.."
items.source:
LKML, 14 Nov 2017, "Re: git pull", https://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/1711.1/04939.html
(also reproduced in `Documentation/maintainer/pull-requests.rst`, "As said by Linus")
items.label: `quoted`
items.from: new (my research). Replaces top-12 #9 and takes the timing point of top-12 #7.

items.title: Clean history: rebase your own private work, never other people's history; merge only for a reason.
items.rule:
People can, and probably should, rebase their own private trees, which is cleanup. Never rebase other
people's history, which destroys it. The rule is about history, not code: a patch you applied yourself is your
history. Once you have published your history, it is no longer private. Don't push out work that is still in the
rebase phase. Don't merge upstream code at random points, and have a reason for merging downstream work. He won't
pull from a tree whose log is full of random merges of his tree.
items.words:
(English original) "I want clean history, but that really means (a) clean and (b) history.
People can (and probably should) rebase their _private_ trees (their own work). That's a _cleanup_. But never
other peoples code. That's a "destroy history"" … "You must never EVER destroy other peoples history. You must
not rebase commits other people did." … "Notice that this really is about other peoples _history_, not about
other peoples _code_." … "once you've published your history in some public site, other people may be using it,
and so now it's clearly not your _private_ history any more." … "Don't expose your crap. This means: if you're
still in the "git rebase" phase, you don't push it out." … "Don't merge upstream code at random points." …
"Slightly more complex version: "Always have a _reason_ for merging downstream stuff"." … "But if I see a lot of
"Merge branch 'linus'" in your logs, I'm not going to pull from you, because your tree has obviously had random
crap in it that shouldn't be there."
items.source:
"Re: [git pull] drm-next", to Dave Airlie, 29 Mar 2009, Message-ID
`alpine.LFD.2.00.0903291409030.3994@localhost.localdomain`, as published at https://lwn.net/Articles/328438/
items.label: `quoted`

items.title: Start small, for an immediate need; don't push your "vision" too hard on the project.
items.rule:
Don't set out to build a large project. Start with a small, trivial one and don't expect it to get
large; expecting that leads to over-design, or to being scared off. Think about the details, not a big picture:
if it doesn't solve a fairly immediate need, it is almost certainly over-designed. Projects have a life of their
own, so don't enforce your "vision" too strongly. You are usually wrong anyway, so be willing to take input,
change direction and admit mistakes.
items.words:
(English original) "Nobody should start to undertake a large project. You start with a small
_trivial_ project, and you should never expect it to get large. If you do, you'll just overdesign and generally
think it is more important than it likely is at that stage. Or worse, you might be scared away by the sheer size
of the work you envision. So start small, and think about the details. Don't think about some big picture and
fancy design. If it doesn't solve some fairly immediate need, it's almost certainly over-designed." … "projects
have a life of their own, and you should _not_ try to enforce your "vision" too strongly on them. Most often
you're wrong anyway, and if you're not flexible and willing to take input from others (and willing to change
direction when it turned out your vision was flawed), you'll never get anything good done. In other words, be
willing to admit your mistakes" · TED2016: "I am not a visionary. I do not have a five-year plan. I'm an
engineer." … "But I'm looking at the ground, and I want to fix the pothole that's right in front of me before I
fall in."
items.source:
Linux Times email interview by Preston St. Pierre, posted 25 Oct 2004 ("Linus Torvalds: 'Desktop
Market has already started'"), Wayback capture
https://web.archive.org/web/20041106193140/http://www.linuxtimes.net/modules.php?name=News&file=article&sid=145 ·
TED2016 transcript (as #10)
items.label: `quoted`

items.title: Patches go to the subsystem maintainer; he trusts the maintainers he pulls from and avoids being the throttle.
items.rule:
Patches go to the subsystem maintainer, and very few go through him directly. People are told to avoid
sending him email even though he is the final arbiter. When he pulls from maintainers, the attention he gives
varies: sometimes he looks quite closely, but as a general rule he trusts them not to send bad patches. In his
own words in 2005, he can process a hundred emailed patches almost as easily as one "as long as I trust the
maintainer". If no parallel-merge tool could be found soon, he would distribute the merging over a few people
rather than be the throttle himself.
items.words:
(English original)
- Doc: "Linus Torvalds is the final arbiter of all changes accepted into the Linux kernel. … He gets a lot of e-mail, and, at this point, very few patches go through Linus directly, so typically you should do your best to -avoid- sending him e-mail."
- Doc: "The amount of attention that Linus pays to specific patches received in a pull operation varies. It is clear that, sometimes, he looks quite closely. But, as a general rule, Linus trusts the subsystem maintainers to not send bad patches upstream."
- His 2005 words: "I can process a hundred emails almost as easily as one, as long as I trust the maintainer (which, when it's used as a BK replacement, I obviously do)." … "at least try to distribute the merging out over a few people rather than making _me_ be the throttle."
items.source:
`Documentation/process/submitting-patches.rst` "Select the recipients for your patch" ·
`Documentation/process/2.Process.rst` §2.3 "How patches get into the Kernel" · LKML, 7 Apr 2005, "Re: Kernel
SCM saga..", https://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/0504.0/1826.html
items.label: the two doc passages are `attributed` (third person, not his); the 2005 lines are `quoted`.

items.title: Take the blame, best of all for someone else; tell the one who really screwed up in private.
items.rule:
When things go wrong, take the blame, and the best way is to take it for someone else. Then let the
developer who really screwed up (if you can find them) know in private. That way they can avoid it next time,
they know they owe you one, and they are likely the person who can fix it. Taking the blame is part of what makes
people trust you.
items.words:
(English original) "Which brings us to the best way of taking the blame: do it for someone
else. You'll feel good for taking the fall, they'll feel good about not getting blamed" … "Then make the
developer who really screwed up (if you can find them) know in private that they screwed up. Not just so they can
avoid it in the future, but so that they know they owe you one. And, perhaps even more importantly, they're also
likely the person who can fix it." … "Taking the blame is also why you get to be manager in the first place. It's
part of what makes people trust you"
items.source: `management-style.rst` §4 "Placing blame"; LWN 2004
items.label: `quoted`. Authorship is by attribution only (see Gaps).

items.title: Don't hide the problem in politeness; never be sanctimonious; apologise. In 2018 he apologised for his personal attacks.
items.rule:
Don't be too polite or subtle, because politeness can end up hiding the problem; make the point
bluntly. Some humour can soften both the bluntness and the moralizing. Don't call people d*ckheads (at least not
in public), and learn to apologise when you do. Worse than that is saying it in a sanctimonious voice, which
people may not give you the chance to apologise for. Alienating people counts as "not reversible". In 2018 he
wrote that his flippant attacks in email, especially the personal ones, were unprofessional and uncalled for,
that this was not OK, and that he needed to change his behaviour.
items.words:
(English original) "Similarly, don't be too polite or subtle about things. Politeness easily
ends up going overboard and hiding the problem, and as they say, "On the internet, nobody can hear you being
subtle". Use a big blunt object to hammer the point in, because you can't really depend on people getting your
point otherwise. Some humor can help pad both the bluntness and the moralizing." … "don't call people d*ckheads
(at least not in public)" / "learn how to apologize when you forgot rule (1)" … "There's one thing people hate
even more than being called "d*ckhead", and that is being called a "d*ckhead" in a sanctimonious voice. The first
you can apologize for, the second one you won't really get the chance." … "It turns out that alienating people is
fairly easy, and un-alienating them is hard. Thus "alienating" immediately falls under the heading of "not
reversible"" · 2018: "My flippant attacks in emails have been both unprofessional and uncalled for. Especially at
times when I made it personal. In my quest for a better patch, this made sense to me. I know now this was not OK
and I am truly sorry." … "hey, I need to change some of my behavior"
items.source:
`management-style.rst` §2 "People", §5 "Things to avoid"; LWN 2004 · LKML, 16 Sep 2018, "Linux
4.19-rc4 released, an apology, and a maintainership note", https://lkml.org/lkml/2018/9/16/167
items.label: `quoted` (management-style authorship by attribution only, see Gaps; the 2018 mail is his)

items.title: For code he has to maintain: short functions that do one thing, shallow nesting, comments that say what and not how.
items.rule:
These are his rules for code he has to maintain. He won't force them on anybody else, but would prefer
them there too. Functions should be short and do one thing. If you need more than 3 levels of indentation, fix
your program. Local variables shouldn't exceed 5–10, because "maybe you'd like to understand what you did 2
weeks from now". Comments should say what the code does, not how. A formatting tool is not a fix for bad
programming.
items.words:
(English original) "Coding style is very personal, and I won't _force_ my views on anybody, but
this is what goes for anything that I have to be able to maintain, and I'd prefer it for most other things too.
Please at least consider the points made here." … "if you need more than 3 levels of indentation, you're screwed
anyway, and should fix your program." … "Functions should be short and sweet, and do just one thing." … "Another
measure of the function is the number of local variables. They shouldn't exceed 5-10, or you're doing something
wrong." … "You know you're brilliant, but maybe you'd like to understand what you did 2 weeks from now." …
"Generally, you want your comments to tell WHAT your code does, not HOW." … "But remember: "indent" is not a fix
for bad programming."
items.source:
`Documentation/CodingStyle` in the Linux 2.0 release (1996), chapters 1, 4, 5 and 6
(https://cdn.kernel.org/pub/linux/kernel/v2.0/linux-2.0.tar.gz). The same sentences are in today's
`Documentation/process/coding-style.rst`, opening and §1, §6, §8, §9.
items.label:
`quoted`, first person ("anything that I have to be able to maintain"). Authorship is by
attribution, not by signature (see Gaps).

items.title: Quantify the claimed win and state its costs; the description must stand alone.
items.rule:
Describe the problem that motivated the patch and its impact on users. If you claim improvements in
performance, memory, stack footprint or binary size, include numbers that back them up. Also describe the
expected downsides, so the reviewer can weigh costs against benefits. Every submission or resubmission carries
its complete description, not just "version N", so that it is self-contained.
items.words:
(English original) "Describe your problem. Whether your patch is a one-line bug fix or 5000
lines of a new feature, there must be an underlying problem that motivated you to do this work." … "Quantify
optimizations and trade-offs. If you claim improvements in performance, memory consumption, stack footprint, or
binary size, include numbers that back them up. But also describe non-obvious costs." … "Describe the expected
downsides of your optimization so that the reviewer can weigh costs against benefits." … "Don't just say that
this is version N of the patch (series)." … "I.e., the patch (series) and its description should be
self-contained."
items.source:
`Documentation/process/submitting-patches.rst` "Describe your changes",
https://docs.kernel.org/process/submitting-patches.html
items.label:
`attributed`: kernel process documentation, not shown to be his words. He is named in the same
document as the final arbiter.

items.title: One logical change per patch, each one buildable; send a long series about 15 at a time.
items.rule:
Put each logical change in its own patch, and keep a single change across many files in one patch.
Each patch should be easy to understand, verifiable, and justifiable on its own merits. In a series, the kernel
should build and run after each patch, because `git bisect` may split the series anywhere. If you cannot condense
the set, post say 15 or so at a time and wait for review and integration.
items.words:
(English original) "Separate each logical change into a separate patch." … "On the other hand,
if you make a single change to numerous files, group those changes into a single patch." … "The point to
remember is that each patch should make an easily understood change that can be verified by reviewers. Each patch
should be justifiable on its own merits." … "take special care to ensure that the kernel builds and runs properly
after each patch in the series. Developers using git bisect to track down a problem can end up splitting your
patch series at any point; they will not thank you if you introduce bugs in the middle." … "If you cannot
condense your patch set into a smaller set of patches, then only post say 15 or so at a time and wait for review
and integration."
items.source: `Documentation/process/submitting-patches.rst` "Separate your changes"
items.label: `attributed`: kernel process documentation, not shown to be his words.
